events.description: US and Taliban sign the withdrawal agreement ('Agreement for Bringing Peace to Afghanistan') in Doha. Part one, section F has the US and allies refrain from the threat or use of force against Afghanistan's territorial integrity or political independence.
Taliban announce a unilateral three-day ceasefire, which the Afghan government welcomes and says it will extend; the Taliban ignore the extension.
Taliban attack in Paktia province kills 14 Afghan soldiers; Zabihullah Mujahid tweets the claim.
US kills senior al-Qaeda leader Faruq al-Qahtani a few days before the Nov 2016 US election.
Rewards for Justice lists Haji Taysir, offering up to $5 million and describing him as deputy emir of manufacturing in Syria.
Reported airstrike in eastern Syria that Iraqi CTS says killed Haji Taysir; unconfirmed.
US soldiers digging at Camp Assad in Mosul unearth containers of potassium cyanide; the host was called to see it.
Al-Naba issue 235 (week 14-20 May) claims 158 ISIS operations worldwide.
Abu Muhammad al-Adnani, first ISIS caliphate spokesman, killed.
Spokesman Abu al-Hassan al-Muhajir killed shortly after al-Baghdadi.
Abu Hamza al-Qurashi releases the speech 'And the Disbelievers Will Know Who Gets the Good End', accusing the Taliban of conspiring with the US and calling the coronavirus divine retribution.
Trump declares the Islamic State defeated (earlier in April 2018, and again in December; the host misspeaks the year as 2009).
Secretary of State Pompeo flies to Doha and meets Taliban political figures.
US offered up to $3 million reward for information on Muhammad Kadir Musa Ramadan (Abu Bakr al-Gharib).
Abu Hamza al-Qurashi speech attacks the Taliban-US deal and al-Qaeda in West Africa.
Secretary of State met Taliban political figures in Doha.

key_claims: The US-Taliban withdrawal deal has the US refrain from the threat or use of force against Afghanistan, which would hamper any return for counterterrorism.
The Taliban refuse to denounce al-Qaeda but are being treated as a counterterrorism partner against ISIS.
ISIS is persistent rather than resurgent: its claimed attack tempo (158 operations in one week, mostly in Iraq and Syria) is in the same areas as during the Iraqi insurgency.
Haji Taysir, if killed, was a long-time ISIS figure overseeing chemical and biological weapons research, but successors are likely ready.
Abu Hamza al-Qurashi's speech accuses the Taliban and al-Qaeda of conspiring with the US against ISIS, attacking them ideologically.
The Taliban are a more robust insurgency than ISKP, which behaves like a terrorist group; many ISKP commanders are ex-Taliban.
The Taliban's Doha diplomacy is legitimizing the Islamic Emirate, and al-Qaeda sees this as a model for its own emirates, such as in West Africa.
The Taliban's three-day ceasefire was unilateral and was not extended, with Afghan officials still alleging violations.
Al-Qaeda endorses the Taliban-US process because it grants legitimacy to Islamic emirates, which it hopes to emulate in West Africa.
ISIS's attacks on al-Qaeda and the Taliban show no grand bargain between the two groups is coming.
Local tactical cooperation between ISIS and al-Qaeda affiliates is plausible because many local commanders were former partners.
The US identified Muhammad Kadir Musa Ramadan as a Jordanian-born senior ISIS media official overseeing daily media operations and provincial content.
He reportedly purged moderates from ISIS propaganda teams and may have been involved in the ultra-radical 'chain takfir' controversy.
